title: Routine caregiver burden screening in memory clinics and outcomes for caregivers and people with dementia: a systematic review
subtitle: Evidence for a decision on routine screening at first visit and every six months
statement: Family caregivers attending the memory clinic are screened for burden inconsistently, and referral to support is patchy. Before committing clinician time to routine screening, the clinic needs to know whether screening followed by referral or support improves caregiver burden, depression or quality of life, or delays care home admission, and whether it works equally for different caregivers. Most studies may test support rather than screening, so the comparison must be defined carefully.
whoAffected: Family caregivers of about 640 people referred each year, the people with dementia they support, and the clinic's five clinicians.
whatHurts: Exhausted caregivers go unrecognised, and support reaches only those who happen to be asked; screening without effective follow-up would add burden to visits without benefit.
currentPractice: Two of five clinicians use a 12-item burden scale; others ask informally or not at all; referral varies.
whyNow: The clinic manager proposes routine screening, and clinician time must be justified.
constraints: Two reviewers (the investigator and a clinic psychologist) with about 50 hours each before May 2027. The hospital library runs the searches. No translation budget; English and Spanish reports only.
patientCenteredGoal: Caregivers who are struggling are recognised and reach support that helps them and the person they care for.
summary: Problem framed as a systematic review of screening followed by referral or support, separating screening from support effects.
